title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models
authors: Shuoran Jiang, Wentao Zhu, Yang Xiang, Dongfeng Li, Yunan Zhang, Mengchen Zhao
abstract: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that LLMs contain low-overlap, functionally specialized subnetworks that can be updated selectively to reduce catastrophic forgetting in continual learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a practical way to make large models adapt to new tasks with lower compute and memory cost by limiting training and optimizer updates to task-relevant regions.
method: Use gradient-attribution profiling to localize cognition-associated subnetworks.
Route each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork.
Restrict parameter updates and optimizer states to the selected regions in CiMEO.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, the method reports the best average performance on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, exam-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning.
infographic.watch_item: Subnetwork routing depends on accurate functional localization, so misassignment or task drift could weaken performance and complicate deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models

title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds
authors: Zhijie Yuan, Lei Sun, Ganzhao Yuan
abstract: Nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds underlies many problems in machine learning and deep learning. However, existing stochastic Riemannian retraction methods often rely on stepsizes that require prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant, a prescribed iteration horizon, or restrictive batch-size choices. We develop {\sf RGR}, a recursive gradient retraction method for stochastic nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds. Instead of recursively updating gradient estimators in changing tangent spaces, {\sf RGR} constructs them in the Euclidean space and subsequently maps them to tangent space, thereby avoiding vector transport. The method comprises three variants: {\sf RGR-SPIDER} for finite-sum optimization and {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} for online stochastic optimization. {\sf RGR-SPIDER} is Lipschitz-free and horizon-free, as its adaptive stepsize requires neither prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant nor a prescribed iteration horizon. {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} are mini-batch and horizon-free methods whose convergence guarantees do not rely on prescribed large batch sizes and whose parameters can be chosen without prior knowledge of the total iteration budget. We show that {\sf RGR-SPIDER} reaches an $\varepsilon$-critical point using $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations and $\mathcal{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient evaluations, where $N$ denotes the number of component functions. For the online setting, {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} achieve iteration complexities of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-4})$, respectively. Experiments on principal component analysis, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal convolutional neural networks demonstrate faster empirical convergence than methods that construct recursive gradient estimators directly in Riemannian tangent spaces.

infographic.key_insight: RGR builds recursive stochastic gradient estimators in Euclidean space and then maps them to the Stiefel tangent space, avoiding vector transport while enabling horizon-free and, in one variant, Lipschitz-free optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a more practical optimizer for large-scale constrained learning tasks such as PCA, matrix completion, and orthogonal neural networks where Stiefel-manifold constraints arise naturally.
method: RGR-SPIDER: finite-sum variant with adaptive, Lipschitz-free and horizon-free stepsizes.
RGR-SRM and RGR-EMA: online stochastic variants that are mini-batch-free/horizon-free and do not require prescribed large batches.
Recursive estimator is formed in Euclidean space first, then projected to the tangent space to avoid vector transport.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports theoretical convergence rates and experiments on PCA, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal CNNs, showing faster empirical convergence than tangent-space recursive methods.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on correct manifold projections/retractions and step-size tuning; benefits may diminish if the Stiefel constraints or stochastic gradients are poorly conditioned.
infographic.paper_title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds

title: Bias Control and Injection for Multi-Agent Aggregation
authors: Sungjae Lee, Soheil Abbasloo, Jabin Koo, Jungseul Ok
abstract: Multi-agent reasoning with large language models (LLMs) raises a central question for collective decision-making: when agents disagree, whose decision should be trusted? Resolving such disagreements is difficult because agents' decisions are susceptible to non-semantic biases such as majority pressure and response-style preferences, which can obscure the quality of the underlying reasoning. Our analysis shows how bias can be both mitigated and exploited: bias control improves initial answer selection, while bias injection elicits decision instability that serves as a reliability signal. Building on these findings, we introduce a test-time aggregation framework that requires neither validation data nor prior knowledge of relative model strength. The framework implements bias control by presenting one style-normalized reasoning trace per distinct answer, and bias injection by placing each aggregating agent's initially selected answer in the minority. Overall, our framework achieves higher average accuracy and better token efficiency than competing non-oracle aggregation methods across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and four heterogeneous LLM combinations. It also improves final-answer accuracy when applied to multi-agent debate and Mixture-of-Agents, without modifying their interaction or synthesis processes.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that controlling and strategically injecting bias can make multi-agent LLM aggregation more reliable when agents disagree.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a test-time, training-free aggregation method that improves answer accuracy and token efficiency without needing validation data or model-strength priors.
method: Normalize each distinct answer into a style-matched reasoning trace before aggregation.
Use bias control to reduce non-semantic effects like majority pressure and response-style preference.
Use bias injection by making each agent’s initial choice the minority to expose decision instability as a reliability signal.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and four heterogeneous LLM pairings, the framework outperforms non-oracle aggregation methods and also improves multi-agent debate and Mixture-of-Agents final-answer accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: The method depends on manipulating presentation order and minority status, so its gains may vary with prompt sensitivity and heterogeneous agent behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Bias Control and Injection for Multi-Agent Aggregation

title: Neural Spline Flow Diffeomorphisms for Pullback Finite Element Methods on Complex Domains
authors: Ioannis Kalogeris, Anaksagoras Spitas, Konstantinos Atzarakis, George Stavroulakis, Vissarion Papadopoulos
abstract: We propose a method for solving partial differential equations on complex domains by learning smooth, invertible mappings from a fixed reference domain using Neural Spline Flows (NSFs). Monotone rational-quadratic spline coupling layers ensure a strictly positive Jacobian determinant by construction, eliminating the need for Jacobian-sign penalties. A diffeomorphic pullback transfers the weak form of the PDE to the reference domain, enabling finite element analysis on reusable structured meshes. To generalize across shapes, a shared NSF is conditioned on low-dimensional latent codes learned through an auto-decoder framework; a subsequent encoder predicts these codes for unseen geometries in a single forward pass. For a given learned map, the pullback preserves the mathematical structure of the PDE and is exactly equivalent to solving on the domain represented by that map. Because the learned domain generally approximates the target geometry, geometric mapping error remains distinct from finite element discretization and quadrature errors. Numerical benchmarks show that sufficiently accurate learned mappings yield reliable finite element solutions. By avoiding repeated generation of unstructured meshes, the method addresses a bottleneck in simulation workflows. The fixed reference mesh also creates opportunities for efficient assembly, memory-aligned data access, and precomputed quadrature. The resulting framework assigns geometric complexity to the neural network while retaining conventional finite element discretization and convergence properties on the learned domain, with overall accuracy also governed by geometric fidelity.

infographic.key_insight: Neural Spline Flows can learn smooth, invertible domain maps so finite element PDEs on complex geometries can be pulled back to a fixed reference mesh without losing diffeomorphic structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can replace repeated unstructured remeshing with reusable structured FEM workflows, improving simulation efficiency while keeping standard discretization machinery intact.
method: Use monotone rational-quadratic spline coupling layers to guarantee a positive Jacobian determinant.
Learn a diffeomorphic map from a reference domain and pull back the PDE weak form to that domain.
Condition a shared NSF on low-dimensional latent codes; an encoder predicts codes for new geometries in one pass.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical benchmarks showing that sufficiently accurate learned mappings produce reliable finite element solutions.
infographic.watch_item: Overall accuracy depends on geometric fidelity, so mapping error can remain a separate source of error from FEM discretization and quadrature.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Spline Flow Diffeomorphisms for Pullback Finite Element Methods on Complex Domains

title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards
authors: Xuanchang Zhang, Tong Zhang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.

infographic.key_insight: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO) removes learner-to-behavior importance weights by optimizing a KL-adjusted log-mean-exp gap over grouped responses, yielding a stable off-policy objective for verifiable-reward RL.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For language-model RL pipelines with stale or offline data, GGPO offers a practical way to train against policy mismatch while controlling variance and preserving reward gains.
method: Minimize a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards across multiple responses to the same prompt.
Derive the objective from KL-regularized policy optimization so the population loss matches the KL-regularized optimality gap on-policy.
Use reference refresh analysis and local reference control to bound final-policy reward under policy staleness and finite data.
infographic.evidence_signal: In experiments on mathematical reasoning, GGPO outperformed GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and fixed offline data, and a default refresh schedule scored 46.58 versus 32.96 with a fixed reference on the five-benchmark weighted average.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on reference refresh and coverage assumptions, so stale references or poor prompt-response coverage can weaken the bound and degrade results.
infographic.paper_title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards

title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles
authors: Swati Gupta, Tianjiao Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand? We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that paying for a higher-fidelity LLM is only worthwhile when its extra accuracy justifies the downstream optimization cost, and proposes adaptive switching policies to decide this automatically.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For data curation and learning pipelines, it offers a cost-aware way to trade off LLM quality against budget while still preserving optimization performance.
method: Restarted cost-aware meta-algorithm that adaptively switches among mixed-fidelity stochastic oracles using known bias.
Budgeted certification scheme with occasional trusted-gradient checks to detect biased sources when bias is unknown.
Subroutines based on biased stochastic gradient extrapolation and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports synthetic and LLM-completion experiments showing the adaptive policy skips expensive LLM calls, reduces cumulative cost, and maintains comparable accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on reliable bias/certification behavior; if trusted-gradient checks are too costly or biased sources are hard to detect, the savings can shrink.
infographic.paper_title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles

title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
authors: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang, Yinyu Ye, Han Zhong
abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $β$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $η$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $β$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $β$ to keep $η/(1-β)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $β_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

infographic.key_insight: In RL with verifiable rewards, momentum helps when the EMA coefficient is chosen large enough to stay in a safe regime, because it preserves a real optimization gain that can otherwise be hidden by sampling noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For practical LLM post-training, tuning momentum upward can improve learning stability and validation accuracy, especially when using SGD+EMA or AdamW at larger model scale.
method: Analyze RLVR with a bandit formulation and bias-corrected EMA momentum.
Prove that, under exact policy gradients, larger β accelerates optimization if overshoot is avoided.
Show that with sampled gradients, fixed β can lose benefit as η shrinks, while increasing β to keep η/(1−β) safe retains a nonvanishing gain.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper validates the theory with bandit simulations and RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen2.5-32B, where increasing β1 improved mean validation accuracy by nearly 2 percentage points.
infographic.watch_item: Momentum gains depend on staying below the overshoot threshold; using too large a β or an unsafe η/(1−β) setting can negate the benefit.
infographic.paper_title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?

title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery
authors: Qiuyu Chen, Qi Wang, Liang Xu, Xin Jin, Baao Xie, Wenjun Zeng
abstract: Mathematical research drives scientific discovery, and recent advances in AI for mathematics have shown that language-model agents can solve challenging problems and develop substantial mathematical proofs. Yet much of today's AI-for-mathematics work centers on obtaining a final answer. This emphasis leaves the exploration behind a result difficult for researchers to understand, while long-running investigations face fragmented context and the risk of unsupported claims propagating across reasoning steps. We present Euler, a human-centered mathematical research system built around a shared, structured representation of the research process. Euler organizes mathematical statements, assumptions, proof dependencies, alternative approaches, failed attempts, and verification evidence into connected research graphs. This representation allows researchers to trace how results are developed and supplies agents with persistent, task-relevant knowledge for planning, collaboration, and verification across sessions. Researchers can also select a graph node linked to a saved team state, revisit the agents' earlier reasoning, and explore alternative directions through continued interaction. We illustrate Euler's capabilities through three mathematical research case studies and describe the implemented system and its software validation.

infographic.key_insight: Euler shifts AI-for-mathematics from single-answer solving to a human-centered, persistent research workflow that records statements, assumptions, proof links, failed attempts, and verification evidence in a shared graph.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The system is relevant for building trustworthy multi-agent scientific assistants because it preserves context across sessions and supports traceability, collaboration, and verification during long research tasks.
method: Builds a structured research graph of mathematical statements, assumptions, dependencies, alternatives, and failures.
Uses the graph as persistent shared memory for multi-agent planning, collaboration, and verification.
Lets researchers revisit saved team states and continue exploring alternative proof paths interactively.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports three mathematical research case studies and software validation to illustrate the system’s capabilities.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract suggests the approach depends on careful graph maintenance and verification; robustness and scalability may be challenging in long, complex investigations.
infographic.paper_title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery

title: Learning Warm Starts for the Simplex Method from Measured Solver Cost
authors: Felix Parker, Danielle A. Ripsman, Emmett Springer, Kimia Ghobadi
abstract: Learned warm starts for the simplex method build starting bases using predictions of which variables will be basic at optimality. Prior work has shown that starting bases predicted by graph neural networks can sharply reduce iteration counts, but the time saved may fall well short of the iterations saved. On 25 classes of linear programs (LPs), we find that a strong supervised basis predictor removes two thirds of the dual simplex's iterations but only a third of its time. Two effects explain the gap: the iterations removed by a good start tend to be cheap, and closeness to an optimal basis does not rank starts by cost. We prove that two starts with equal overlap with an optimal basis and equal pivot counts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor that grows with the square root of the number of rows. Empirically, across the starts of one LP, the pivot count explains 71% of the variance of log solve time, while the CPU instruction count explains 98.5%. We introduce CostStart, which uses supervised prediction for the basis and trains a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose, per LP, how many predicted columns to use, which algorithm and pricing rule to run, and whether to warm-start at all. On unseen LPs of the training classes, including LPs four times the training size, CostStart roughly halves the solve time relative to the solver's default start and is 1.4 to 2.2 times as fast as two published methods retrained on the same data.

infographic.key_insight: Warm-start quality for simplex is not determined just by fewer pivots: the same-quality start can have very different linear-algebra cost, so the paper learns starts using measured solver cost, not iteration count alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For LP solvers in practice, optimizing the warm start can cut wall-clock time substantially, making learned initialization more useful for real workloads than pivot reduction alone.
method: Predict a candidate optimal basis with a supervised model.
Train a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose how many predicted columns to use, plus algorithm and pricing rule.
Optionally skip warm-starting when it is not cost-effective.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 25 LP classes, the method cuts dual-simplex iterations by about two-thirds but only about one-third of solve time; on unseen LPs it roughly halves solve time versus the default start.
infographic.watch_item: A warm start that looks close in basis overlap may still be expensive, so deploying this approach requires cost-aware evaluation and hardware-sensitive measurement.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Warm Starts for the Simplex Method from Measured Solver Cost

title: Why Shallow Neural Networks Learn Sinusoidal Components First: An Orthogonal Polynomial Dynamics Framework
authors: Yanyang Xiao
abstract: Neural networks often learn low-frequency components before high-frequency ones --- a phenomenon called spectral bias or termed F-principle. Many numerical studies have demonstrated this phenomenon, and theoretical studies have sought to explain it. However, several goals remain insufficiently addressed: (1) explaining spectral bias asymptotically, including its origin and why the preferred components are generally sinusoidal; (2) extending the explanation to general activation functions, such as sigmoid and ReLU; (3) making weak assumptions about the data distribution; (4) avoiding aliasing effects, such as those arising in finite-domain Fourier analysis; and (5) developing a theoretical framework applicable to arbitrary networks. We address these goals theoretically by analyzing the eigenvalue decay and eigenvector shapes of the dynamics matrix H, which arises when we expand the network output as a general Fourier series (GFS) in an orthogonal polynomial basis and express the gradient-descent dynamics of the GFS coefficients as ordinary differential equations. The graded structure of H enables an intuitive explanation of spectral bias, while orthogonal polynomial theory helps us analyze how learning bias depends on the activation function and, potentially, the network architecture.

infographic.key_insight: Shallow neural networks learn low-frequency, sinusoidal-like components first because the gradient-descent dynamics matrix has a graded structure whose eigenvalues decay and eigenvectors align with orthogonal-polynomial Fourier modes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework gives a more general theory of spectral bias that can help engineers predict training dynamics across activation functions and data distributions, not just in Fourier-domain toy settings.
method: Expand network outputs as a general Fourier series in an orthogonal polynomial basis.
Derive gradient-descent dynamics for the series coefficients as an ODE system with dynamics matrix H.
Analyze H's eigenvalue decay and eigenvector shapes to explain why smooth sinusoidal components emerge first.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is theoretical, using asymptotic analysis of the dynamics matrix H rather than new experimental data in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is analytical and depends on the polynomial-basis approximation, so practical validation and numerical stability may vary for specific architectures and datasets.
infographic.paper_title: Why Shallow Neural Networks Learn Sinusoidal Components First: An Orthogonal Polynomial Dynamics Framework

title: Two Sample Sizes in Test-Time LLM Ensembling: Buffered ERM and Minimax Theory
authors: Zhi Zhang, Arash A. Amini
abstract: Test-time scaling can improve the performance of large language models by generating multiple answers to a question and aggregating them. Weighted ensembles extend this idea by drawing answers from several models, with the weights determining how often each model is used. Learning these weights from a training dataset involves two sample sizes: $Q$ labeled questions and $N$ generations per model and question. We study their interplay through the clean risk, the population error of the ensemble's infinite-generation voting rule. Under a margin condition with exponent $β$, we show that empirical risk minimization (ERM) with a calibrated margin buffer achieves excess risk of order $Q^{-1/2}+N^{-β/2}$, up to logarithmic factors, for fixed numbers of models and candidate answers. To investigate the optimality of this dependence on $Q$ and $N$, we analyze a simplified submodel with two models and two possible answers per question. We characterize its minimax excess risk up to constants by a Hellinger modulus for a binomial-mixture experiment. Polynomial approximation and spectral analysis reveal three regimes. When questions are relatively scarce, the $Q^{-1/2}$ term governs learning and the general buffered ERM is optimal. In an intermediate regime, pooling generation counts across questions improves upon estimating each answer distribution separately, with only logarithmic gains from additional questions. With sufficiently many questions, the minimax excess risk reaches an $N^{-β}$ identification floor that persists even with infinitely many questions. The submodel's lower bounds also apply to general ensembles, matching the buffered-ERM upper bound up to logarithmic factors when questions are scarce and in parts of the intermediate regime. Questions remain about the transitions between regimes and the construction of matching pooled estimators for general ensembles.

infographic.key_insight: Learning test-time ensemble weights depends on two sample sizes, and buffered ERM achieves near-optimal excess risk of order Q^{-1/2}+N^{-β/2} under a margin condition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For LLM ensembling, this gives a practical scaling law for how many labeled questions (Q) and generations per model (N) are needed to improve voting-based test-time performance.
method: Buffered ERM adds a calibrated margin buffer to stabilize weight learning.
A simplified two-model/two-answer submodel is used to derive minimax lower bounds.
Hellinger-modulus, polynomial approximation, and spectral analysis expose three sample-size regimes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical excess-risk bounds and minimax characterizations, rather than empirical experiments, with rates depending on Q, N, and the margin exponent β.
infographic.watch_item: The sharp transitions between the identified regimes are not fully resolved, and a matching pooled estimator for general ensembles is still open.
infographic.paper_title: Two Sample Sizes in Test-Time LLM Ensembling: Buffered ERM and Minimax Theory

title: Minimizing Age of Incorrect Information in Pull-Based Remote Estimation of a Markov Source
authors: Ismail Cosandal, Sennur Ulukus, Nail Akar
abstract: In this paper, we consider a discrete-time pull-based remote estimation system involving an information source and a remote monitor where the information source is a finite-state irreducible discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) process. In this system, the remote monitor sends a pull request towards the source which responds by sampling its process so as to transmit the sampled values towards the monitor through a delay channel, encapsulated in information packets. We consider i) zero delay (ZD) and ii) unit delay (UD) channels, where the packet transmission times are zero and one slot, respectively. For remote estimation, we use the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator, and for quantifying its performance, we use the mean age of incorrect information (MAoII) which is a recently proposed freshness and mismatch metric that penalizes an incorrect estimation along with its duration. Our goal is to obtain pull policies so as to minimize MAoII under a long-run sampling rate constraint. For the ZD model, we propose a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) formulation of the problem, which allows us to find the optimum observation-dependent pull policy. On the other hand, the UD channel prevents the monitor from possessing perfect information on the actual AoII process at any given time, and the SMDP formulation of the ZD channel cannot readily be used for the UD model. For the system with the UD channel, we first provide a numerical algorithm to calculate the MAoII and the average sampling rate for a given observation-dependent pull policy. For the optimization of the underlying remote estimation system, we use the joint distribution of the age and source processes to be obtained from the history of all observations, termed as belief. Subsequently, we propose a belief-dependent policy obtained via the belief-MDP formulation and a constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) algorithm.

infographic.key_insight: The paper minimizes Mean Age of Incorrect Information (MAoII) in pull-based remote estimation of a Markov source by optimizing when the monitor should request samples under delay and sampling-rate constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a principled control policy for freshness-critical remote monitoring systems where outdated or wrong state estimates can directly affect decision-making.
method: Formulate the zero-delay case as a semi-Markov decision process to obtain an optimal observation-dependent pull policy.
For unit-delay channels, compute MAoII and average sampling rate numerically using the joint age-source distribution from the full observation history (belief).
Use a belief-MDP with constrained deep reinforcement learning to learn a belief-dependent pull policy under sampling constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical optimization for the zero-delay model and numerical evaluation plus algorithmic development for the unit-delay model, including computation of MAoII and average sampling rate.
infographic.watch_item: The unit-delay setting relies on belief-state estimation and deep RL, which may be computationally heavy and sensitive to approximation error or model mismatch.
infographic.paper_title: Minimizing Age of Incorrect Information in Pull-Based Remote Estimation of a Markov Source

title: Evolution algebras: a survey of results and a list of open problems
authors: Ivan Kaygorodov, Cándido Martín González, Antonio Viruel
abstract: Evolution algebras, introduced by J. P. Tian as an algebraic model of non- Mendelian inheritance, are commutative algebras with a basis whose distinct elements multiply to zero. The first part of the paper surveys the theory: low-dimensional classifica- tions, structure theory, nilpotency, automorphisms and derivations, directed graphs and random walks, infinite-dimensional and dynamical aspects, and embedding theorems. The second part is a unified list of fifty open questions and eleven new conjectures, each accompanied by the available evidence; two of the conjectures and one of the questions are settled here. We also prove several new observations, most of them formally verified in the proof assistant Lean (see Section 2.1.11): every finite group is the automorphism group of a simple evolution algebra over every field, and | Aut(A)|/ dim A takes every positive ratio- nal value on simple evolution algebras over every field; infinitude of the automorphism group of nilpotent algebras, the possible numbers of idempotents of real perfect evolution algebras, a Galois-theoretic criterion for the existence of idempotents in dimension two, the average number of idempotents over finite fields, and a perfect evolution algebra whose automorphism group is a non-split extension.

infographic.key_insight: This survey shows that evolution algebras have a rich structure theory and unexpectedly flexible symmetry behavior, with many foundational questions resolved and several open problems now sharply organized.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For theorem proving and formalized algebra, the paper is notable because it combines broad mathematical classification with Lean-verified results, making it a strong benchmark for interactive proof and symbolic algebra systems.
method: Surveyed core theory: classification, nilpotency, automorphisms/derivations, graph and dynamical viewpoints.
Collected 50 open questions and 11 conjectures, then resolved some by new proofs.
Formally verified several new observations in Lean, especially about automorphism groups and idempotents.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports new theorem-level results, including Lean-formalized proofs, plus evidence-backed conjectures and open questions rather than experimental data.
infographic.watch_item: Many results are structural and field-dependent, so automated reasoning or implementation must carefully track assumptions such as dimension, simplicity, perfectness, and the base field.
infographic.paper_title: Evolution algebras: a survey of results and a list of open problems

title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret
authors: Mohammad Pedramfar, Siamak Ravanbakhsh
abstract: Many modern learning systems are used not to select a single best action, but to sample diverse high-quality outputs. Examples include entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, RLHF, and reward-guided generative modeling. Motivated by these settings, we study tilted sampling: an online learning problem in which the goal is to sample from the Gibbs distribution induced by an unknown reward function. We define sampling regret as the temperature-normalized cumulative KL divergence between the learner's distribution and the Gibbs target, corresponding to the suboptimality gap in entropy-regularized reward maximization. Our framework generalizes recent sampling-based and KL-regularized formulations in bandits and reinforcement learning. Our main contribution is a general regret framework that captures the different uncertainty structure of tilted sampling and classical regret minimization. While standard regret scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ due to first-order uncertainty, sampling regret is governed by squared confidence widths, yielding logarithmic-in-$T$ regret in standard settings at fixed temperature. We develop sampling analogues of UCB and Thompson sampling (UCS and TS$^2$) and provide unified regret decompositions that explain and extend recent logarithmic guarantees, including the first Bayesian sampling-regret decomposition based on new bounds for posterior-random Gibbs distributions. Our results show that learning to sample from a soft-optimal distribution is statistically distinct from learning to identify a hard optimum.

infographic.key_insight: Learning to sample from an unknown Gibbs-optimal distribution is statistically different from choosing a single best action, and this shift turns regret from O(\sqrt{T}) into logarithmic growth under standard conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For entropy-regularized RL, RLHF, and reward-guided generation, this gives a principled way to design samplers that stay close to the desired soft-optimal policy rather than merely optimizing one action.
method: Defines sampling regret as temperature-normalized cumulative KL to the target Gibbs distribution.
Develops two sampling analogues of bandit algorithms: UCS and TS^2.
Provides unified regret decompositions, including a Bayesian decomposition for posterior-random Gibbs targets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical regret guarantees, including logarithmic-in-T bounds at fixed temperature and the first Bayesian sampling-regret decomposition.
infographic.watch_item: The logarithmic guarantees rely on fixed-temperature and standard uncertainty assumptions, so performance may degrade or require new analysis in low-temperature or highly misspecified settings.
infographic.paper_title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret

title: Adaptive Randomized Neural Networks for PDEs: Structure-Aware Feature Redistribution and Residual-Driven Block Enrichment
authors: You Yang, Fei Wang
abstract: Randomized neural networks retain an output-linear least-squares solve, but globally sampled random features may fail to capture the spatial and scale structure of PDE solutions. We propose SFRBE--RaNN, a two-stage adaptive trial-space construction. SFR redistributes a fixed feature budget according to regional indicator masses and adapts regional weight scales through low-dimensional residual-based optimization. RBE constructs nonredundant enrichments by screening multiple activation families, removing represented response directions, and selecting the smallest admissible prefix. For solution-dependent operators, candidates are screened with a frozen operator and accepted only after nonlinear residual verification. For fixed linear problems, we establish an exact discrete residual-reduction identity and a conditional solution-error estimate. Building on this identity, we combine safeguarded SFR with RBE capture factors to derive a finite-horizon error bound involving baseline best approximation and empirical consistency, together with a conditional random-search success-probability bound. Numerical experiments on localized, multiscale, and nonlinear space--time problems demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

infographic.key_insight: SFRBE--RaNN adaptively redistributes random feature capacity and adds only nonredundant enrichments to better match PDE spatial scales, while preserving a fast output-linear solve.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical way to improve accuracy on localized, multiscale, and nonlinear PDEs without abandoning the computational efficiency of randomized neural networks.
method: SFR: reallocates a fixed feature budget by regional indicator mass and tunes regional scales via residual-based low-dimensional optimization.
RBE: screens multiple activation families, removes already-represented response directions, and selects the smallest admissible enrichment prefix.
For nonlinear operators, candidates are first screened with a frozen operator and then accepted only if they pass nonlinear residual verification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments on localized, multiscale, and nonlinear space-time problems, and also states exact residual identities and conditional error/success-probability bounds for fixed linear cases.
infographic.watch_item: The adaptive screening and verification steps add implementation complexity, and the theoretical guarantees are conditional rather than universal.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Randomized Neural Networks for PDEs: Structure-Aware Feature Redistribution and Residual-Driven Block Enrichment

title: IneqAgent: Agentic Inequality Proving in Lean with Symbolic Computation
authors: Gaolei He, Jinhui Li, Ruobing Zuo, Xia Zeng, Zhengfeng Yang
abstract: Formal inequality proving requires mathematical reasoning and exact computation, often connected through intermediate lemmas and goal reformulations. We introduce IneqAgent, an agentic framework combining LLM reasoning with symbolic computation for inequality proving in Lean4. Lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and symbolic backend selection. Complementary sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends produce exact certificates for local Lean proof generation. The agent integrates these proofs with LLM-generated steps and uses Lean feedback to construct complete proofs checked against the original theorem statements. On four benchmarks, IneqAgent with DeepSeek-V4-Flash solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%), achieving the highest overall success rate among the evaluated methods. Across four backbones, it achieves higher success rates at low LLM inference cost thresholds than Direct Agent using the same backbone, with lower mean inference costs over each method's successful runs. We also obtain Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture in dimensions four and five, and certify the Holens--Djokovic $(4,4)$ inequality, implying Merris's conjecture in dimension four.

infographic.key_insight: IneqAgent combines LLM planning with exact symbolic backends in Lean4 to prove inequalities by constructing and checking lemma-level proof steps.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework shows how agentic search plus certified computation can improve reliability and reduce inference cost for formal mathematical proving systems.
method: Lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and backend choice.
Uses symbolic backends such as sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference substitution to generate exact certificates.
Integrates backend proofs with LLM-generated steps and Lean feedback to complete verified proofs.
infographic.evidence_signal: On four benchmarks, DeepSeek-V4-Flash with IneqAgent solved 175 of 186 problems (94.09%), with higher success at low inference-cost thresholds and lower mean cost on successful runs across four backbones.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of symbolic backend selection and Lean integration, so difficult goals may still require careful engineering and may not generalize uniformly across domains.
infographic.paper_title: IneqAgent: Agentic Inequality Proving in Lean with Symbolic Computation

title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
authors: Neil Walton
abstract: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.

infographic.key_insight: A rate-transfer method turns finite-time Lyapunov bounds for an associated SDE into finite-time convergence rates for stochastic gradient algorithms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a calculus-based way to prove and predict convergence behavior for SGD-type optimizers, including new variants, without requiring a full bespoke discrete-time analysis.
method: Model the stochastic gradient method with an associated SDE.
Verify a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE using calculus.
Transfer the resulting finite-time Lyapunov estimate into a convergence-rate bound for the algorithm.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and extends to new algorithms via SDE-based calculus arguments.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on moment and smoothness conditions plus a suitable SDE approximation, so rate guarantees may be sensitive to modeling assumptions.
infographic.paper_title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus

title: Towards Learning-Guided Discovery of Extremal Geometric Constructions: A PatternBoost Study
authors: Deepak Ajwani, Paula Carroll, Rishikesh Gajjala, Ananta Manoranjan, Ryan O'Connor, Rajiv Raman
abstract: Extremal constructions play a central role in the design and analysis of algorithms. Integrality-gap instances expose the limitations of relaxations, while hard configurations reveal structural sources of computational difficulty. Such constructions, however, are still typically discovered through a slow, manual process. This paper investigates how machine learning can accelerate their discovery to support algorithm design and analysis. We build on PatternBoost, a framework alternating local search with generation from a trained transformer, using its Axplorer implementation to investigate three problems: integrality gaps for maximum independent set of rectangles, integrality gaps for stabbing unit squares with axis-parallel lines, and hard instances for recursive guillotine cutting. By exploring candidate representations, local search operations, and surrogate models used to rank candidates before exact verification, we carefully adapt the framework to these combinatorial geometry problems.While naive representations and search strategies fail to find non-trivial instances, our tailored adaptation discovers numerous non-trivial constructions. For stabbing unit squares, the method reaches a gap of $20/13\approx 1.54$, improving on the literature's best known lower bound of $3/2$. Purely automated search converges rapidly and then plateaus, prompting the question of what is required to push the bound higher still. We find that initial instance diversity plays an important role: with modest expert input via a structured staircase construction, the system reaches an improved integrality gap of $14/9\approx 1.555$. These results demonstrate that machine learning and domain expertise can be combined to discover new extremal constructions that advance algorithmic lower bounds.

infographic.key_insight: A PatternBoost-style loop of local search plus transformer-guided generation can discover new extremal geometric constructions, especially when the search space and representations are tailored to the problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work offers a practical template for using learning-guided search to strengthen lower bounds and stress-test algorithmic relaxations in geometric optimization.
method: Adapted PatternBoost/Axplorer to three combinatorial geometry tasks.
Designed problem-specific candidate representations, local moves, and surrogate ranking models.
Used exact verification to filter generated candidates and measure true integrality gaps.
infographic.evidence_signal: On stabbing unit squares with axis-parallel lines, the automated search found a gap of 20/13 ≈ 1.54, and with structured expert-initialized instances it improved further to 14/9 ≈ 1.555.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends strongly on representation quality and initial diversity; naive setups plateau quickly and may miss stronger constructions.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Learning-Guided Discovery of Extremal Geometric Constructions: A PatternBoost Study

title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Omar Adalat, Edwin Hamel-De le Court, Francesco Belardinelli
abstract: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns rational synthesis into a MARL learning problem: find strategy profiles that satisfy each agent’s temporal objective while remaining stable under game-theoretic solution concepts like Nash or subgame-perfect equilibrium.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a model-free way to verify and optimize temporal-logic requirements in multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, relevant to autonomous coordination, verification, and safe control.
method: Compile each agent’s PLTLf objective into a reward automaton and learn strategies with Nash-Q in a stochastic MARL setting.
Use simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds to certify satisfaction probabilities.
Check approximate best responses to assess strategic stability under the chosen equilibrium notion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach is empirically evaluated on 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence and certification are conditional on tabular assumptions and finite-sample approximations, so scalability and estimation error may limit deployment in larger systems.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems

title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
authors: Fei Wu, Zhenrong Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jun Du
abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.

infographic.key_insight: VASPO combines a critic-based PPO value estimate with privileged self-teacher signals, using each where it is strongest to improve math-reasoning training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For reasoning-model training, it offers a practical way to blend dense supervision and return-aware optimization, improving accuracy without relying only on GRPO-style signal scaling.
method: Compute PPO token-level advantages from a critic that predicts continuation returns at student-generated prefixes.
Use a self-teacher with privileged information to modulate selected positive advantages through bounded probability ratios.
Exploit complementary dynamics: critic is stronger near the end of responses, while self-teacher is strongest early and rebounds at the end.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improved mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 points on Qwen3-4B and 1.81 points on OLMo3-7B, and achieved the best mean accuracy on Knights and Knaves.
infographic.watch_item: Because the method depends on careful coordination between critic estimates and self-teacher weighting, instability or miscalibration in either component could reduce the benefit.
infographic.paper_title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation
